summary: This document defines two DHCPv6 messages, Reconfigure-Request and Reconfigure-Reply. A relay agent sends a Reconfigure-Request to tell a server that configuration information has changed so it can send a Reconfigure message. The server answers with a Reconfigure-Reply.

eli5.summary: A helper tells the main office "something changed, please update everyone," and the office confirms it got the note.

questions: how a relay agent triggers dhcpv6 reconfigure
how does a relay trigger dhcpv6 reconfigure
subtitle: Lets a DHCPv6 relay agent tell the server that configuration changed, so the server can reconfigure clients.

tldr.problem: When a relay agent supplies configuration data that later changes, the DHCPv6 server has no way to notice, so it never sends a Reconfigure message to the affected clients.
tldr.mechanism: The relay sends a new Reconfigure-Request message naming the affected clients and their link. The server acknowledges with a Reconfigure-Reply carrying a status code and then builds the Reconfigure messages.
tldr.outcome: A relay can now trigger reconfiguration itself, with retransmission, rate limiting and relay authentication to keep it safe. Servers reject these requests unless configured to accept them.

facts.label: Retransmission
facts.value: IRT 1 sec, MRT 10 secs, MRC 5, MRD 0

today: RFC 6977 is a Proposed Standard, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata for this unit. It defines the way a relay agent triggers DHCPv6 reconfiguration.

sections.title: The Problem: Silent Configuration Changes
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 relay agent can pass configuration data to the server in the Relay-Supplied Options option (RSOO) defined in RFC 6422. The server then hands that data back to the requesting client. The RFC's example is a broadband network where the Network Access Server (NAS) embeds the relay agent and learns a DS-Lite tunnel name from a RADIUS server.

That data can change later. In the RFC's example, a Change-of-Authorization (CoA) exchange between the NAS and a Dynamic Authorization Client (DAC) server changes it (see RFC 5176); the text also notes that any other out-of-band mechanism could trigger such a change. The DHCPv6 server has no means of detecting the change, so it cannot send a Reconfigure message to the client.
sections.eli5: The front desk learns new rules from head office, but the manager never hears about the change. So the manager never tells the guests.

sections.title: The Solution: Reconfigure-Request and Reconfigure-Reply
sections.content:
The RFC defines two new DHCPv6 messages. A Reconfigure-Request is sent by the relay to the server as soon as the configuration data in an RSOO has changed. If the server is configured to support this mode, it builds a Reconfigure-Reply to acknowledge the request, and a normal Reconfigure message that travels to the client inside a Relay-Reply.

The relay must already have a record of the client. How it stores that state is out of scope, but the RFC says means to recover state after a failure (stable storage, or DHCPv6 Bulk Leasequery from RFC 5460) need to be supported.

The Reconfigure-Reply exists because the alternative is fragile. A relay could watch for Reconfigure messages instead, but a server might delay them because of rate limiting, or fail for only some clients. An explicit reply lets the relay retransmit a corrected request and stop when no clients remain to be reconfigured.
sections.eli5: The helper sends a note and waits for a "got it" reply. Without the reply it would have to guess whether the manager did anything.

sections.title: Message Types and the Link Address Option
sections.content:
Two message type codes are defined: RECONFIGURE-REQUEST (18) and RECONFIGURE-REPLY (19). Both use the same message format as in Section 6 of RFC 3315.

The new Link Address Option has option code OPTION_LINK_ADDRESS (80) and an option-len of 16 octets. It holds an IPv6 address that the server uses to identify the link where the client sits. The relay MUST use a value equivalent to the one it used when relaying the client's messages, meaning an address on-link for the client's network link. To guard against poor implementations, it SHOULD use the very same value it sent before.
sections.eli5: The Link Address Option is like writing the street name on the note, so the manager knows which neighbourhood the guests live in.

sections.title: How the Relay and Server Behave
sections.content:
Relay. After a change, the relay finds the affected clients, sets msg-type to RECONFIGURE-REQUEST and generates a transaction ID. It MUST include one or more Client Identifier Options and a Link Address Option. It MAY add a Relay Identifier Option, the updated configuration in an RSOO, a Reconfigure Message Option, and other options it would normally insert. If the client list would exceed the maximum message size, it MUST send several requests. With several servers configured, it builds one request per server.

Retransmission follows Section 14 of RFC 3315 with IRT 1 sec, MRT 10 secs, MRC 5 and MRD 0. The relay MAY drop clients from later retransmissions but MUST NOT add any. It SHOULD judge success by the Reconfigure-Reply, not by a Reconfigure message arriving first.

Server. A server MUST be configurable to accept or reject these requests, and the default is to reject. It copies the transaction ID into a Reconfigure-Reply, includes its Server Identifier Option and MUST include a Status Code Option. It then builds Reconfigure messages following Section 19.1 of RFC 3315.

Intermediate relays MUST be configurable to accept or reject Reconfigure-Request messages from other relays. The default is to accept.
sections.eli5: The helper writes down who needs to know and where they live, and re-sends the note a few times if no reply comes. The manager only acts if the manager has been told that such notes are allowed.

sections.title: Validation and Status Codes
sections.content:
A server MUST discard a Reconfigure-Request that lacks a Client Identifier Option, lacks a Link Address Option, or carries a Server Identifier Option that does not match its own. Clients silently discard any Reconfigure-Request, and clients and servers silently discard any Reconfigure-Reply. A relay discards a Reconfigure-Reply with a mismatched transaction ID, or one missing a Server Identifier Option or Status Code Option.

The Status Code in the reply tells the relay what happened:

  • UnspecFail MUST be returned if the request is malformed.
  • NotAllowed MUST be returned if the server is not configured to allow Reconfigure-Request.
  • NotConfigured MUST be returned if the server has no record of the link.
  • Success is returned if the request validates, along with a list of Client Identifier Options for clients that will not get a Reconfigure (for example, no record of the client or no Reconfigure support negotiated). Success can therefore be returned even if no client is reconfigured.

The relay may end its attempt on NotAllowed, NotConfigured or Success, or try a corrected request after UnspecFail. It treats a client as handled if at least one reply does not list that client.
sections.eli5: The manager answers with a code: "fine," "not allowed," "I don't know that street," or "your note was garbled." The helper decides what to do next from that code.

sections.title: Rate Limiting and Security
sections.content:
The relay MUST rate-limit Reconfigure-Request messages, and the maximum request size SHOULD be configurable with a default MUST of 1280 octets. The server MUST rate-limit the Reconfigure messages it sends because of these requests.

Because a Reconfigure can be abused, for example to control the timing of a DHCPv6 renewal, the server MUST have some way to decide that the relay is trusted. Servers and relays MUST implement relay message authentication as in Section 21.1 of RFC 3315, and servers MAY apply a policy based on the Relay Identifier Option. Where the path is not under the server administrator's control, IPsec is necessary to prevent spoofing. Servers MUST silently discard requests from unknown relay agents, and relays SHOULD guard against being used for denial-of-service attacks on servers.
sections.eli5: The manager only listens to helpers it trusts, and nobody is allowed to send too many notes too fast.

items.label: RECONFIGURE-REQUEST
items.desc: Relay to server: configuration changed, please reconfigure these clients.

items.label: RECONFIGURE-REPLY
items.desc: Server to relay: acknowledges the request with a status code.

items.label: OPTION_LINK_ADDRESS
items.desc: Option holding an IPv6 address that identifies the client's link (16 octets).
